questions.question: Two granola bars are exactly the same size. The first bar is cut into 4 equal parts and Ravi eats 1 part. The second bar is cut into 8 equal parts and Jae eats 2 parts. Did the two children eat the same amount of granola bar?
options: Yes — each of the 8 parts is half the size of a fourth, so 2 of them match 1 of them: 1/4 = 2/8.
No — the second bar is cut into 8 parts and 8 is more than 4, so 2/8 has to be the bigger amount.
No — to change 1/4 you add 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom to get 2/5, and 2/5 is not the same as 2/8.
No — Jae ate 2 parts and Ravi ate only 1 part, so Jae ate more.
questions.explain: Multiply the numerator and denominator of 1/4 by 2 to get 2/8, so both children ate the same amount. The usual trap is thinking more pieces means more food — cutting into 8 parts makes each part smaller.

questions.question: Two pizzas are the same size. One pizza is cut into 6 equal slices and 3 slices are taken. The other pizza is cut into 2 equal halves and 1 half is taken. Are 3/6 and 1/2 equivalent fractions?
options: No — 3/6 is the bigger fraction because 6 slices is more slices than 2.
Yes — 3 and 6 share the factor 3, and dividing both by 3 gives 1/2, so exactly half of each pizza was taken.
No — 3 taken is not the same as 1 taken, and equivalent fractions must have the same numerator.
No — 1/2 turns into 2/3 when you count up by 1 on the top and on the bottom, so 1/2 matches 2/3, not 3/6.
questions.explain: Divide the numerator and denominator of 3/6 by the common factor 3 to get 1/2, so the two amounts are equal. Remember that equivalent fractions almost never have matching top numbers — it is the size of the pieces that changes.

questions.question: Two ribbon strips are the same length. The first strip is divided into 10 equal pieces and 6 pieces are coloured red. The second strip is divided into 5 equal pieces and 3 pieces are coloured red. Is the same length of ribbon red on both strips?
options: No — 3/5 becomes 4/6 when you add 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom, and 4/6 is not 6/10.
No — 6/10 covers more of the strip, because that strip is cut into 10 pieces instead of only 5.
Yes — 6 and 10 both divide by the common factor 2 to give 3/5, so 6/10 = 3/5 and the same length is red.
No — 6 red pieces is double 3 red pieces, so twice as much of the first strip is red.
questions.explain: Dividing both 6 and 10 by the common factor 2 gives 3/5, so the red parts are equal in length. The trap is counting pieces instead of thinking about size: tenths are smaller than fifths, so it takes 6 of them to match 3 fifths.

questions.question: Two identical water bottles have measuring marks on them. One bottle is marked into 12 equal sections and is filled up to 8 sections. The other bottle is marked into 3 equal sections and is filled up to 2 sections. Which statement is true?
options: The 8/12 bottle holds more water, because 12 sections is more sections than 3.
They are not equivalent, because 2/3 becomes 3/4 when you go up by 1 on the top and the bottom.
They are not equivalent, because 8 sections filled and 2 sections filled are different numbers.
They are equivalent — 8 and 12 both divide by the common factor 4, which gives 2/3, so both bottles are 2/3 full.
questions.explain: Dividing 8/12 by the common factor 4 gives 2/3, so both bottles hold the same amount of water. Watch out for judging by the denominator alone — a bottle with more marks just has thinner sections.

questions.question: Nadia wants to decide whether 4/6 and 6/9 are equivalent. Which statement gives the right answer with correct reasoning?
options: They are equivalent — dividing 4/6 by the common factor 2 gives 2/3, and dividing 6/9 by the common factor 3 also gives 2/3.
They are not equivalent — 6/9 is the larger fraction because ninths come from a bigger denominator than sixths.
They are not equivalent — 4/6 becomes 5/7 if you count up by 1 on the top and bottom, so it can never reach 6/9.
They are not equivalent — only fractions with the same denominator can ever be equivalent.
questions.explain: Simplify both fractions and compare: 4/6 = 2/3 and 6/9 = 2/3, so they are equivalent. Counting up by 1 on the top and bottom does not keep the value — you must multiply or divide both parts by the same number.

questions.question: Which fraction is NOT equivalent to 2/5?
questions.explain: Multiplying the numerator and denominator of 2/5 by 2, 3 and 4 gives 4/10, 6/15 and 8/20, so those three are all equivalent. The fraction 3/6 comes from adding 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom, and that changes the value — 3/6 is one half, which is more than 2/5.

questions.question: Maya says that 10/12 and 5/6 are equivalent fractions. Liam says they are not. Who is right, and why?
options: Liam — 5/6 must be smaller, because sixths come from a smaller denominator than twelfths.
Liam — going from 5/6 to 10/12 adds 5 to the top and 6 to the bottom, and since those are different numbers the value changed.
Maya — 10 and 12 share the common factor 2, and dividing both by 2 gives 5/6, so 10/12 = 5/6.
Liam — the numerators 10 and 5 are different, so the two fractions cannot name the same amount.
questions.explain: Divide 10/12 by the common factor 2 to get 5/6, so Maya is right. Equivalent fractions are made by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number, never by adding to them.

questions.question: Which method correctly shows that 7/8 and 14/16 are equivalent?
options: Add 7 to the numerator and 7 to the denominator of 7/8, because both parts should grow by the same amount.
Multiply only the denominator of 7/8 by 2, because only the size of the pieces changes.
Compare the denominators — 16 is greater than 8, so 14/16 is the greater fraction.
Multiply the numerator and the denominator of 7/8 by 2, because 7 x 2 = 14 and 8 x 2 = 16.
questions.explain: Multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by 2 turns 7/8 into 14/16, so the fractions are equivalent. Adding 7 to each part would give 14/15, and doubling only the denominator would give 7/16 — both of those change how much of the whole you have.

questions.question: At a Burnaby school bake sale, Priya brought a tray of 20 muffins and 8 of them had blueberries. Owen brought a tray of 15 muffins and 6 of them had blueberries. Priya says the two trays have the same fraction of blueberry muffins. Is she correct?
options: No — 6/15 goes to 7/16 and then 8/17 when you count up, so it never becomes 8/20.
No — 8 blueberry muffins is more than 6 blueberry muffins, so Priya's tray has the greater fraction.
Yes — 8/20 divides by 4 to give 2/5, and 6/15 divides by 3 to give 2/5, so both trays are 2/5 blueberry.
No — Priya's fraction is bigger, because her tray has 20 muffins and 20 is more than 15.
questions.explain: Simplify each fraction first: 8/20 = 2/5 and 6/15 = 2/5, so the trays match. The common trap is comparing the raw counts of muffins instead of comparing each count with the size of its own tray.

questions.question: Ella tells her class, 'I know that 2/3 = 3/4, because I just added 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom.' Which response corrects her best?
options: She is right, because she did exactly the same thing to the numerator and to the denominator, which always keeps a fraction's value.
Her rule does not work — on a pizza cut into 12 slices, 2/3 is 8 slices but 3/4 is 9; to keep the value you multiply both parts, so 2/3 = 4/6.
She is wrong only because 3/4 is bigger — 4 is a bigger denominator than 3, so any fraction with 4 on the bottom is bigger than one with 3.
She is right this time, but the rule only works when the numerator is smaller than the denominator, as it is in both 2/3 and 3/4 here.
questions.explain: Adding the same number to the top and bottom changes the value: 2/3 of 12 slices is 8, while 3/4 of 12 slices is 9. To make an equivalent fraction you must multiply both the numerator and denominator by the same number, as in 2/3 = 4/6.

questions.question: On a Grade 5 field trip to Stanley Park, 9 of the 12 students in Group A brought a rain jacket, and 6 of the 8 students in Group B brought one. Which group had the greater fraction of students with rain jackets?
options: Group A, because 12 students is more than 8 students, so 9/12 is the greater fraction.
Group B, because going from 6/8 to 9/12 you add 3 to the top and 4 to the bottom, which makes 9/12 a different, smaller fraction.
Neither — 9/12 and 6/8 both simplify to 3/4, so the two groups had the same fraction of students with rain jackets.
Group B, because only 2 students there were missing a jacket while 3 students were missing in Group A.
questions.explain: Simplify both fractions: 9/12 divides by 3 to give 3/4, and 6/8 divides by 2 to give 3/4, so the groups are tied. Comparing the number of students who forgot, or the size of the groups, does not tell you the fraction — you must compare each count with its own group total.

questions.question: A community garden in Victoria has two rain tanks. The small tank holds 20 L when full and has 12 L in it. The large tank holds 50 L when full and has 30 L in it. Are the two tanks filled to equivalent fractions of their capacity?
options: No — the large tank is fuller, because 50 L is a bigger whole, so 30/50 is a bigger fraction.
No — from 12/20 to 30/50 the top rose by 18 and the bottom by 30, and those are different numbers, so the fractions are not equivalent.
No — 30 L is much more water than 12 L, so the large tank is filled to a bigger fraction.
Yes — 12/20 divides by 4 to give 3/5, and 30/50 divides by 10 to give 3/5, so both tanks are 3/5 full.
questions.explain: Write each amount as a fraction of its own tank and simplify: 12/20 = 3/5 and 30/50 = 3/5, so both tanks are equally full. More litres does not mean a greater fraction, and equivalence is never checked by looking at what was added.
